scope: Eight conceptual Linux configuration explanations with sixteen selected comparisons. Existing commands, prerequisites, applicability, IDs, kinds, mappings and connections are preserved and unreviewed.

decisions.previousSummary: A binary carries a capability (cap_setuid, cap_dac_override, ...) that yields root.
decisions.previousDescription: File capabilities split root into discrete powers attached to a binary, and several are root-equivalent. cap_setuid+ep on an interpreter lets it call setuid(0) and drop a root shell. cap_dac_override reads or writes any file (edit /etc/shadow). cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, and cap_sys_module are similarly decisive. Enumerate with getcap and match the capability to its abuse.
decisions.summary: Understand individual Linux privileges and thread capability sets.
decisions.description: Linux capabilities divide traditional superuser privileges into individually controlled units. Capabilities are attributes of threads, and the kernel consults a thread's effective capability set when checking privileged operations. The capability model distinguishes individual permissions from the broad concept of running as root.

claims.text: Linux capabilities separate traditional superuser privileges into independently enabled units and are a per-thread attribute.
claims.section: Linux man-pages, capabilities(7) — DESCRIPTION: opening capability definition

claims.text: The effective capability set is the set the kernel uses for a thread's permission checks.
claims.section: Linux man-pages, capabilities(7) — Thread capability sets — Effective

decisions.previousSummary: Append a UID-0 account with a known password to a writable passwd file.
decisions.previousDescription: If /etc/passwd is writable, add your own root-equivalent account. A passwd line's second field can hold a crypt(3) password hash of any format ($1$ MD5, $5$ SHA-256, $6$ SHA-512, $y$ yescrypt), which takes precedence over /etc/shadow, so append an entry with UID 0 and a password hash you generated, then su to it. Even without a hash field, a writable passwd lets you point an existing account at a shell or clear a root password prompt.
decisions.summary: Understand the account records and permissions of /etc/passwd.
decisions.description: /etc/passwd describes system login accounts. Its records include the login name, user and primary group IDs, account information, home directory and login program. The Linux manual recommends making this account information readable by users while restricting writes to the superuser. Account information and authority to modify it are separate concerns.

claims.text: /etc/passwd describes login accounts and records the login name, UID, primary GID, account information, home directory and login program.
claims.section: Linux man-pages, passwd(5) — DESCRIPTION: account records and field definitions

claims.text: The Linux manual recommends general read access to /etc/passwd and superuser-only write access.
claims.section: Linux man-pages, passwd(5) — DESCRIPTION: opening file-permission guidance

decisions.previousSummary: Crack the root hash if shadow is readable; replace it if writable.
decisions.previousDescription: A misconfigured /etc/shadow is a direct route to root. If it is readable, extract the root hash and crack it offline. If it is writable, replace the root hash with one you generated and su in with the matching password. Either way the account model is untouched, so the change is subtle compared with editing /etc/passwd.
decisions.summary: Understand protected password records and password-aging information.
decisions.description: /etc/shadow stores account password information and optional password-aging information. The shadow-utils manual describes fields for the last password change, minimum and maximum password ages, warnings and expiration. It states that regular users must not be able to read the file if password security is to be maintained.

claims.text: /etc/shadow stores account password information together with optional password-aging information.
claims.section: shadow-utils, shadow(5) — DESCRIPTION: opening file definition and aging fields

claims.text: The shadow-utils manual requires that regular users cannot read /etc/shadow to maintain password security.

decisions.previousSummary: A root cron job, its script, or a directory it uses is writable by you.
decisions.previousDescription: Cron and systemd timers run jobs as their owner, usually root. Enumerate /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.*, and per-user crontabs, and watch with pspy to catch jobs not listed in a file. If the invoked script is writable, append a reverse shell or a setuid copy of bash; if only the directory is writable, drop a file the job globs in; if the job calls a command by relative name, that is a PATH hijack. Your payload runs as root on the next tick.
decisions.summary: Distinguish user crontabs from system job definitions.
decisions.description: Cron schedules work from crontab definitions. In Cronie, a user crontab's commands run as its owner. The system crontab and files in /etc/cron.d use an additional field to identify the account for a job. A schedule and the account that executes its work are distinct parts of a job definition.

claims.text: Cronie runs commands in a user crontab under the account that owns that crontab.
Cronie system crontabs use an additional username field to identify the account for each job.

decisions.previousSummary: A writable unit file, or its ExecStart target, runs your command as root.
decisions.previousDescription: Services run as root through systemd units. If a unit file, a drop-in it includes, or the binary/script named in ExecStart is writable, set ExecStart to your payload (or edit the target) and start or wait for the service. A writable timer that triggers such a unit is the scheduled variant. Relative-path or writable-PATH ExecStart lines are the same class of bug as cron PATH hijacking.
decisions.summary: Distinguish timer activation from service execution identity.
decisions.description: A systemd timer activates another unit, ordinarily the service with the corresponding name. The activated service has its own execution configuration. systemd documents user and group identity settings for system services and distinguishes them from services run by a user's service manager. The timer schedule alone does not describe the service's identity.

claims.text: A systemd timer activates another unit and defaults to the service with the matching name.
claims.section: systemd, systemd.timer(5) — DESCRIPTION: matching unit and default service

claims.text: systemd documents service user and group identity separately and distinguishes system services from services run by a user's service manager.
claims.section: systemd, systemd.exec(5) — USER/GROUP IDENTITY — User=, Group=

decisions.previousSummary: Plant a setuid-root binary on a share exported no_root_squash.
decisions.previousDescription: NFSv3 trusts the UID the client supplies, and an export configured no_root_squash keeps a client root as root on the share. From a machine where you are root (often your own attack host), mount the export, write a setuid-root shell onto it, and run that binary back on the target as your unprivileged user to become root. /etc/exports (or exportfs -v) shows the no_root_squash flag; showmount -e only lists exported paths, not their options, so use it to find candidate exports and confirm no_root_squash by mounting a candidate as root, creating a test file, and verifying from the target that it is owned by uid 0.
decisions.summary: Understand NFS export definitions and client access settings.
decisions.description: The NFS server export table describes server filesystems made available to clients. Its entries associate export points with allowed clients and export options. The exports manual treats the exported filesystem, client access list and options as separate parts of the server's configuration.

claims.text: /etc/exports records local filesystems on an NFS server that are available to NFS clients.
An NFS export entry identifies an export point, allowed clients and export options for those clients.

decisions.previousSummary: Access to the Docker daemon is root: mount the host and break out.
decisions.previousDescription: The Docker daemon runs as root, so any principal that can talk to it (membership in the docker group, or a readable /var/run/docker.sock) is effectively root on the host. Run a container that bind-mounts the host filesystem and chroot into it, or write a setuid binary onto the host from inside. No container escape bug is needed; this is the daemon working as designed.
decisions.summary: Distinguish Docker daemon management from container identity.
decisions.description: The Docker daemon receives API requests and manages images, containers, networks and volumes. Docker also supports rootless mode, in which the daemon and containers run without root privileges inside a user namespace. Describing Docker security therefore requires distinguishing the daemon, its operating mode and the containers it manages.

claims.text: The Docker daemon accepts API requests and manages images, containers, networks and volumes.
claims.section: Docker, Docker overview — Docker architecture — The Docker daemon

claims.text: Docker rootless mode runs both the daemon and containers without root privileges inside a user namespace.
claims.section: Docker, Rootless mode — Opening definition; How it works

decisions.previousSummary: The lxd group drives the root LXD daemon; mount the host in a container.
decisions.previousDescription: Membership in the lxd group (the group owning the LXD daemon Unix socket) lets you drive the LXD daemon, which runs as root. Import a small image, launch a privileged container that bind-mounts the host root filesystem, and read or write it as root from inside the container. Like the Docker socket, this is the daemon trusting the group rather than a vulnerability.
decisions.summary: Distinguish LXD instance types and container user identities.
decisions.description: LXD supports system containers and virtual machines. System containers use the host kernel, while a virtual machine supplies its own kernel. LXD's unprivileged containers use a user namespace, mapping container UID 0 to an unprivileged user outside the container. Container identity and administrative access to the instance manager are different concepts.

claims.text: LXD supports system containers using the host kernel and virtual machines using their own kernel.
claims.section: Canonical LXD, Containers and VMs — Opening instance types; Virtual machines vs. system containers

claims.text: An unprivileged LXD container uses a user namespace that maps its UID 0 to an unprivileged user outside the container.
